summary: Defines the standard algorithm TCP senders are required to use to compute and manage their retransmission timer. It was later replaced by RFC 6298.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP must decide how long to wait before sending something again if no reply arrives. This is the formula for that wait.

questions: how does tcp compute retransmission timeout
how does tcp compute the retransmission timeout

subtitle: The formula TCP senders must use to decide how long to wait before sending unacknowledged data again.

tldr.problem: TCP needs a retransmission timer to ensure delivery when no feedback arrives from the receiver, and the length of that timer (the RTO) has to be set sensibly.
tldr.mechanism: The sender tracks a smoothed round-trip time (SRTT) and its variation (RTTVAR), sets RTO to SRTT plus four times RTTVAR, never below 1 second if it follows the SHOULD, and doubles the RTO each time the timer expires.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2988 turned the algorithm from a SHOULD in RFC 1122 into a MUST. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 6298.

today: RFC 2988 is obsoleted by RFC 6298, which is now the place to look for the RTO algorithm. This document was a Proposed Standard published in November 2000.

sections.title: Why TCP Needs a Retransmission Timer
sections.content:
TCP uses a retransmission timer to make sure data is delivered even when the remote receiver sends no feedback. The duration of this timer is the RTO (retransmission timeout). RFC 1122 already said the RTO should be calculated as outlined in Jacobson's 1988 paper.

This document codifies that algorithm and upgrades the requirement to support it from a SHOULD to a MUST. It does not change how TCP begins sending after the timer expires; that is outlined in RFC 2581.

A sender may be more conservative than the algorithm allows, but a TCP MUST NOT be more aggressive.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP sends little packages and waits for a thank-you note. If no note comes, it sends the package again, so it needs a rule for how long to wait.

sections.title: The Basic Algorithm
sections.content:
The sender keeps two state variables: SRTT (smoothed round-trip time) and RTTVAR (round-trip time variation). It also assumes a clock granularity of G seconds. The rules are:

  • Before any round-trip time (RTT) measurement exists, the sender SHOULD set RTO to 3 seconds.
  • On the first measurement R, MUST set SRTT = R, RTTVAR = R/2 and RTO = SRTT + max(G, K*RTTVAR), where K = 4.
  • On each later measurement R', MUST update RTTVAR = (1 - beta) * RTTVAR + beta * |SRTT - R'| first, then SRTT = (1 - alpha) * SRTT + alpha * R', and then recompute RTO. The constants SHOULD be alpha = 1/8 and beta = 1/4.
  • If the computed RTO is under 1 second, it SHOULD be rounded up to 1 second.
  • A maximum MAY be placed on RTO, provided it is at least 60 seconds.

The order matters: the old SRTT is used when updating RTTVAR. The RFC explains that a large minimum RTO keeps TCP conservative and avoids spurious retransmissions, while allowing that future research might show a smaller minimum is acceptable.

Implementations with a heartbeat timer may yield a value between 2.5 and 3 seconds for the initial RTO. A lower bound of 2.5 seconds is acceptable if the timer never expires sooner, and a heartbeat timer of granularity G SHOULD NOT go below 2.5 + G seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP keeps a running average of how long replies usually take, plus a note of how much that time wobbles. It waits the average plus a few wobbles, and never less than one second.

sections.title: Taking RTT Samples and Clock Granularity
sections.content:
TCP MUST use Karn's algorithm for taking RTT samples: samples MUST NOT come from segments that were retransmitted, because it is ambiguous whether the reply answered the first copy or a later one. The only safe exception is when the TCP timestamp option is in use, since it removes that ambiguity.

A TCP implementation MUST take at least one RTT measurement per RTT, unless Karn's algorithm prevents it. For modest congestion windows, research suggests timing every segment does not give a better estimator. How to adjust alpha and beta when many samples are taken per RTT is described as an open research question.

There is no requirement on the clock granularity G. If the K*RTTVAR term equals zero, though, the variance term MUST be rounded to G seconds. Experience shows that finer clocks (100 msec or less) perform somewhat better than coarser ones.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP only times a reply when it is sure which message the reply belongs to, like not guessing which of two identical letters a friend is answering. A finer clock helps it time things more exactly.

sections.title: Managing the RTO Timer
sections.content:
An implementation MUST manage its timers so a segment is never retransmitted less than one RTO after its previous transmission. The RECOMMENDED procedure is:

  • When a packet containing data is sent (including a retransmission) and the timer is not running, start it to expire after RTO seconds.
  • When all outstanding data has been acknowledged, turn the timer off.
  • When an ACK acknowledges new data, restart the timer for RTO seconds.

When the timer expires, the sender retransmits the earliest unacknowledged segment, then MUST set RTO = RTO * 2 (exponential backoff), then restarts the timer with the doubled value. The maximum from the basic algorithm may cap the doubling.

Once a new RTT measurement is obtained after a retransmission, the normal computation runs again and can collapse the RTO back down. A TCP MAY also clear SRTT and RTTVAR after backing off several times, since they are likely bogus by then; they are then initialized from the next sample as for a first measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: Start a stopwatch when you send something. If the thank-you arrives, reset it. If time runs out, send again and wait twice as long next time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who can add delay to a packet or its acknowledgment could make a sender compute a large RTO. The RFC notes that the ability to add delay usually comes with the ability to drop the packet, so it is hard to see what extra damage this would do.

The Internet relies on correct RTO behavior, together with the algorithms in RFC 2581, to preserve stability and avoid congestion collapse. An attacker could try to push RTO to an unsafe low value by forging acknowledgments, but this requires correct spoofing, which is difficult unless the attacker can monitor traffic on the path. Even then, the sender still backs off when a packet is lost to real congestion, so the RFC sees little to gain from it.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could try to make TCP wait too long or too little. But anyone who can mess with the mail in that way can already do worse things, so this adds little danger.

items.title: SRTT
items.text: Smoothed round-trip time, updated with alpha = 1/8.

items.title: RTTVAR
items.text: Round-trip time variation, updated with beta = 1/4.

items.title: RTO
items.text: SRTT + max(G, K*RTTVAR) with K = 4; at least 1 second (SHOULD).

items.title: Initial RTO
items.text: 3 seconds until the first RTT measurement.
